questions.question: What is Mendel's Law of Segregation (First Law of Inheritance)?

options.A: During gamete formation, the two alleles for a heritable character segregate from each other so that each gamete carries only one allele
options.B: All dominant genes are inherited together on the same chromosome
options.C: Recessive traits are permanently destroyed in the F1 generation
options.D: Chromosomes do not separate during meiosis

questions.explanation: Mendel's First Law states that homologous allele pairs separate during anaphase I of meiosis, packaging one allele into each haploid gamete.

questions.question: What is the expected phenotypic ratio in the $F_2$ generation of a classic Mendelian Monohybrid cross with complete dominance?

options.A: 3 Dominant : 1 Recessive
options.B: 1 Dominant : 2 Intermediate : 1 Recessive

questions.explanation: Crossing heterozygous monohybrids ($Aa \times Aa$) yields a genotypic ratio of $1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa$ and a phenotypic ratio of $3:1$.

questions.question: What is the expected phenotypic ratio in the $F_2$ generation of a Mendelian Dihybrid cross involving two independently assorting unlinked genes?
questions.explanation: Dihybrid cross ($AaBb \times AaBb$) produces 9 dominant-dominant : 3 dominant-recessive : 3 recessive-dominant : 1 recessive-recessive.

questions.question: What type of genetic cross is performed to determine whether an individual showing a dominant phenotype is homozygous dominant ($AA$) or heterozygous ($Aa$)?

options.A: Test Cross (crossing the unknown individual with a homozygous recessive $aa$ individual)
options.B: Backcross with a homozygous dominant individual
options.C: Reciprocal cross between two wild-type individuals
options.D: Polyhybrid selfing cross

questions.explanation: A test cross pairs the unknown dominant organism with a homozygous recessive tester; a 1:1 progeny ratio reveals heterozygosity, while 100% dominant confirms homozygosity.

questions.question: In incomplete dominance (such as in Mirabilis jalapa / 4 o'clock flowers), what is the phenotypic ratio in the $F_2$ generation from a cross between red ($RR$) and white ($rr$) parents?

options.A: 1 Red : 2 Pink : 1 White
options.B: 3 Red : 1 White
options.C: All Red
options.D: 9 Red : 7 White

questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance, heterozygotes display an intermediate blended phenotype (pink), making genotypic and phenotypic ratios identical ($1:2:1$).

questions.question: What is 'Codominance' as observed in human ABO blood group inheritance?

options.A: Both alleles ($I^A$ and $I^B$) are fully and simultaneously expressed in the heterozygous phenotype without blending (Blood Group AB)
options.B: One allele completely masks the other
options.C: Neither allele produces functional antigens
options.D: Alleles blend to form a new intermediate antigen

questions.explanation: In codominance, heterozygous $I^A I^B$ individuals express both A-antigen and B-antigen glycoproteins simultaneously on red blood cell membranes.

questions.question: How many alleles govern the ABO blood group system in human populations, and how many distinct genotypes can they produce?

options.A: 3 multiple alleles ($I^A, I^B, i$) producing 6 distinct genotypes and 4 phenotypes (A, B, AB, O)
options.B: 2 alleles producing 3 genotypes
options.C: 4 alleles producing 8 genotypes
options.D: 6 alleles producing 12 genotypes

questions.explanation: The ABO locus has 3 multiple alleles; combinations produce 6 genotypes ($I^A I^A, I^A i, I^B I^B, I^B i, I^A I^B, ii$) and 4 phenotypes.

questions.question: Which human blood group is known as the 'Universal Donor' for red blood cell transfusions because its erythrocytes lack both A and B surface antigens?

options.A: Blood Group O negative ($O^-$)
options.B: Blood Group AB positive ($AB^+$)
options.C: Blood Group A positive ($A^+$)
options.D: Blood Group B negative ($B^-$)

questions.explanation: Type $O^-$ erythrocytes lack A, B, and Rh (D) antigens, minimizing the risk of agglutination when transfused into any recipient.

questions.question: Which human blood group is the 'Universal Recipient' for RBCs because the plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies?

options.A: Blood Group AB positive ($AB^+$)
options.B: Blood Group O negative ($O^-$)
options.C: Blood Group B positive ($B^+$)
options.D: Blood Group A negative ($A^-$)

questions.explanation: Type $AB^+$ individuals lack circulating anti-A, anti-B, and anti-Rh antibodies, allowing safe reception of packed red cells of any ABO/Rh type.

questions.question: What severe hemolytic disease of the newborn (Erythroblastosis Fetalis) can occur during a second pregnancy when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus?

options.A: Maternal anti-Rh (anti-D) IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal Rh-positive red blood cells
options.B: Fetal red blood cells attack maternal liver cells
options.C: Maternal insulin passes into the fetus causing hypoglycemia
options.D: Fetal hemoglobin mutates into sickle cell hemoglobin

questions.explanation: Rh incompatibility sensitizes $Rh^-$ mothers during the first $Rh^+$ delivery; subsequent $Rh^+$ pregnancies face transplacental IgG destruction of fetal RBCs.

questions.question: What preventive medical injection is administered to an Rh-negative mother within 72 hours of delivering an Rh-positive baby to prevent sensitization?

options.A: Anti-D Immunoglobulin (RhoGAM)
options.B: Erythropoietin
options.C: Oxytocin
options.D: Insulin

questions.explanation: RhoGAM binds and destroys stray fetal $Rh^+$ erythrocytes before the maternal immune system can recognize them and produce memory B cells.

questions.question: What is 'Epistasis' in non-allelic gene interactions?

options.A: A phenomenon where the expression of an allele at one gene locus masks or alters the phenotypic expression of an allele at a completely different locus
options.B: The linkage of genes on the same chromosome
options.C: A mutation that causes sterility
options.D: The blending of maternal and paternal traits

questions.explanation: Epistasis involves inter-genic masking, such as the Bombay blood group where homozygous recessive $hh$ masks the expression of $I^A$ and $I^B$ alleles.

questions.question: What is 'Polygenic Inheritance' (Quantitative inheritance), responsible for continuous traits such as human skin color, height, and wheat kernel color?

options.A: A single phenotypic trait controlled additively by the cumulative effects of multiple independent genes
options.B: A single gene affecting multiple unrelated phenotypic traits
options.C: Inheritance mediated exclusively through mitochondrial DNA
options.D: A trait governed by environmental temperature alone

questions.explanation: Polygenic traits are controlled by multiple additive genes, resulting in a continuous bell-shaped normal distribution curve across a population.

questions.question: What is 'Pleiotropy'?

options.A: The phenomenon where a single gene influences multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits or organ systems
options.B: Multiple genes controlling one single trait
options.C: The complete absence of dominance in alleles
options.D: The duplication of an entire chromosome set

questions.explanation: Pleiotropy occurs when a single mutation affects multiple body systems (e.g., Marfan syndrome causing fibrillin defects in eyes, aorta, and skeleton).

questions.question: What are 'Linked Genes' in classical genetics?

options.A: Genes physically located close to each other on the same chromosome that tend to be inherited together, violating independent assortment
options.B: Genes located on different non-homologous chromosomes
options.C: Genes that code for ribosomal subunits
options.D: Genes that undergo spontaneous deletion

questions.explanation: Syntenic genes located near each other on the same chromosome travel together into gametes unless separated by homologous crossing over.

questions.question: During which stage of Meiosis does homologous genetic Crossing Over (recombination) occur, breaking linkage between syntenic genes?

options.A: Pachytene stage of Prophase I
options.B: Metaphase II
options.C: Anaphase I
options.D: Telophase II

questions.explanation: Crossing over occurs during pachytene of prophase I between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes aligned in synaptonemal complexes.

questions.question: In the chromosomal sex-determination system of humans and Drosophila fruit flies, what chromosome combinations determine female and male sexes?

options.A: XX determines female, XY determines male
options.B: ZZ determines female, ZW determines male
options.C: XX determines male, XO determines female
options.D: Sex is determined by ploidy

questions.explanation: Humans use the XX/XY system: females are the homogametic sex ($XX$) and males are the heterogametic sex ($XY$).

questions.question: In birds, butterflies, and some reptiles, which sex-determination system operates?

options.A: ZZ-ZW system (Females are heterogametic ZW, Males are homogametic ZZ)
options.B: XX-XY system
options.C: Haplodiploidy
options.D: Environmental temperature determination only

questions.explanation: In birds, females produce two different types of gametes ($Z$ and $W$), while males produce only $Z$-bearing sperm ($ZZ$).

questions.question: Which master sex-determining gene located on the short arm of the human Y chromosome triggers testis development in male embryos?

options.A: SRY Gene (Sex-determining Region Y)
options.B: FOXP2 Gene
options.C: BRCA1 Gene
options.D: HoxA1 Gene

questions.explanation: The SRY gene encodes Testis-Determining Factor (TDF), which directs undifferentiated bipotential gonads to develop into testes.

questions.question: Why are X-linked recessive genetic disorders (such as Hemophilia A and Red-Green Color Blindness) far more prevalent in males than females?

options.A: Males are hemizygous ($XY$) and have only one X chromosome; a single mutant allele on the X chromosome will be expressed phenotypically
options.B: The Y chromosome actively silences dominant genes
options.C: Females cannot produce blood clotting factors
options.D: Estrogen destroys normal red-green cone receptors

questions.explanation: Males have only one X chromosome ($XY$); without a second X to provide a normal dominant allele, any recessive X-linked mutation is directly expressed.

questions.question: What is 'Hemophilia A' ('Royal Disease') caused by genetically?

options.A: An X-linked recessive mutation causing a deficiency of blood coagulation Factor VIII
options.B: An autosomal dominant mutation in Factor V
options.C: A deletion of the entire Y chromosome
options.D: A deficiency of Vitamin C in liver cells

questions.explanation: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder caused by deficiency or dysfunction of clotting Factor VIII.

questions.question: What is 'Red-Green Color Blindness' (Daltonism)?

options.A: An X-linked recessive condition characterized by a deficiency or abnormal spectrum of red (protan) or green (deutan) retinal cone photopigments
options.B: An infection of the optic nerve by bacteria
options.C: The complete absence of rod cells in the retina
options.D: An age-related clouding of the lens

questions.explanation: Genes encoding red and green opsin cone photopigments reside on the X chromosome; recessive mutations impair red-green discrimination.

questions.question: What is a 'Sex-Limited Trait'?

options.A: A trait encoded by autosomal genes that is phenotypically expressed in only one sex due to anatomical or hormonal differences (e.g., milk yield in cows, beard growth in men)
options.B: A gene located on the Y chromosome only
options.C: A disease that kills 100% of male embryos
options.D: A mutation that prevents meiosis

questions.explanation: Sex-limited traits are present in both sexes' genomes on autosomes but expressed exclusively in one sex due to sex steroid regulation or anatomy.

questions.question: What is a 'Sex-Influenced Trait' (such as pattern baldness in humans)?

options.A: An autosomal trait whose phenotypic dominance is influenced by the sex of the individual (e.g., dominant in males due to testosterone, recessive in females)
options.B: A trait transmitted strictly from father to son on the Y chromosome
options.C: A chromosomal inversion on chromosome 21
options.D: A trait that skips three generations

questions.explanation: Pattern baldness allele $B$ behaves as dominant in heterozygous males ($Bb$ are bald due to high dihydrotestosterone), but recessive in females ($Bb$ non-bald).

questions.question: What is a 'Barr Body' in mammalian cytogenetics (Lyon Hypothesis)?

options.A: An inactive, heterochromatinized X chromosome condensed against the nuclear envelope in somatic cells of normal females
options.B: The condensed Y chromosome found in sperm cells
options.C: A chromosomal centromere during metaphase
options.D: An extra copy of chromosome 21

questions.explanation: Mary Lyon showed that one X chromosome in female somatic cells is randomly inactivated (forming a Barr body) for dosage compensation with males.

questions.question: What genetic disorder is characterized by Trisomy 21 ($47, +21$), presenting with intellectual disability, simian crease, epicanthic folds, and cardiac defects?

options.A: Down Syndrome
options.B: Turner Syndrome
options.C: Klinefelter Syndrome
options.D: Edwards Syndrome

questions.explanation: Down syndrome is an autosomal aneuploidy caused by nondisjunction of chromosome 21 during maternal meiosis, resulting in 47 chromosomes.

questions.question: What is 'Turner Syndrome' cytogenetically, and what are its clinical features?

options.A: Monosomy X ($45, XO$), presenting in phenotypic females with short stature, webbed neck, ovarian dysgenesis (streak ovaries), and primary amenorrhea
options.B: Trisomy of chromosome 18
options.C: An extra Y chromosome in males ($47, XYY$)
options.D: A deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5

questions.explanation: Turner syndrome is the only viable human monosomy ($45, X0$), characterized by absent Barr bodies, sterile streak gonads, and webbed neck.

questions.question: What is 'Klinefelter Syndrome' cytogenetically, and what are its clinical manifestations?

options.A: $47, XXY$ karyotype in phenotypic males, characterized by testicular atrophy, azoospermia, gynecomastia, and tall eunuchoid stature
options.B: $45, XO$ karyotype in females
options.C: Trisomy of chromosome 13
options.D: Complete deletion of the X chromosome

questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome involves an extra X chromosome in males ($47, XXY$), displaying a positive Barr body, hypogonadism, and infertility.

questions.question: What is 'Nondisjunction' during meiotic division?

options.A: The failure of homologous chromosomes (in meiosis I) or sister chromatids (in meiosis II) to separate properly, producing aneuploid gametes
options.B: The exchange of genetic material during crossing over
options.C: The complete duplication of mitochondrial DNA
options.D: The degradation of the nuclear envelope

questions.explanation: Nondisjunction produces gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers ($n+1$ or $n-1$), which upon fertilization yield trisomy or monosomy.

questions.question: What is 'Cri du Chat' (Cat's Cry) syndrome caused by cytogenetically?

options.A: A terminal or interstitial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 ($5p^-$)
options.B: Trisomy of chromosome 13 (Patau syndrome)
options.C: An extra X chromosome in females ($47, XXX$)
options.D: Inversion of chromosome 9

questions.explanation: Cri du chat syndrome is caused by a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, producing microcephaly and a high-pitched cat-like infant cry.

questions.question: What is 'Huntington's Disease' in human genetics?

options.A: An autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an unstable expanded trinucleotide repeat ($CAG$) in the huntingtin gene
options.B: An X-linked recessive bleeding disorder
options.C: A bacterial infection of the spinal cord
options.D: A dietary deficiency of vitamin D

questions.explanation: Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat expansion disorder ($CAG > 36$) causing progressive striatal atrophy and chorea.

questions.question: What is 'Cystic Fibrosis' caused by genetically in human physiology?

options.A: An autosomal recessive mutation in the CFTR gene (most commonly $\Delta F508$), impairing chloride transport and producing thick viscous mucus
options.B: An extra chromosome 18
options.C: An X-linked dominant deficiency of insulin
options.D: A chromosomal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22

questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR chloride channel gene, causing thick desiccated secretions in lungs, pancreas, and sweat glands.

questions.question: What is 'Amniocentesis' in prenatal genetic screening?

options.A: The transabdominal aspiration of amniotic fluid containing desquamated fetal cells for karyotyping and biochemical genetic analysis
options.B: Measuring maternal blood pressure during labor
options.C: An ultrasound scan measuring fetal bone length
options.D: Injecting antibiotics directly into the umbilical cord

questions.explanation: Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid around 15–18 weeks gestation to culture fetal cells for chromosomal karyotyping and biochemical testing.

questions.question: What is 'Chorionic Villus Sampling' (CVS) compared to amniocentesis?

options.A: A biopsy of chorionic villi performed earlier (10 to 12 weeks gestation) to extract fetal trophoblast tissue for rapid karyotyping
options.B: Testing maternal urine for protein
options.C: Extracting fetal blood from the placenta at delivery
options.D: A postnatal hearing test for infants

questions.explanation: CVS samples chorionic villi transcervically or transabdominally earlier in pregnancy (first trimester) to detect fetal chromosomal abnormalities.

questions.question: What does a standardized pedigree chart use to represent an affected male individual?

options.A: A fully shaded square (■)
options.B: An unshaded circle (○)
options.C: A shaded circle (●)
options.D: An unshaded triangle (△)

questions.explanation: In clinical genetics pedigree charts, squares represent males, circles represent females, and fully shaded symbols indicate affected individuals.
